title: Just visited the Jewish Museum in center city Philly, next to the liberty bell and constitution…
text: Just visited the Jewish Museum in center city Philly, next to the liberty bell and constitution center. Learned a lot about the jewish migration to America from colonial times to the modern era. The emphasis was on America, with much less about the holocaust or the middle east conflict. I was surprised to hear about the broad distribution to various parts of the US. The facility was user-friendly and the displays and presentation was quite good. I would encourage folks to check it out!

title: We live in a capitalist society and have largely embraced the "invisible power of free markets"…
text:
We live in a capitalist society and have largely embraced the "invisible power of free markets" as per Milton Friedman, et al.  Interestingly, there is strong backlash on both sides of the aisle, as evidenced by the rise of economic populism.  The limits of the free-market system are nicely illustrated in several important areas such as cost of housing (or supply limited shortage of housing units), lagging in emergent areas such as solar panels, inadequate domestic manufacturing in key areas such as chips, famously in healthcare, etc. Markets alone cannot adequately address these areas and requires a thoughtful strategy by our elected leaders for effective partnership between gov't and corporate world.

There is an emerging school of thought for a more active role for gov't in lowering barriers so private enterprise can use the magic of competition for both innovation and meet demand in key sectors.  This would extend to circumventing certain regs in zoning for housing as well as a more aggressive policy on anti-competitive practices by corporate titans (i.e. Kroger - Albertson's merger in groceries, Google in search, etc.).

Of course, this will get the usual pushback from pure market traditionalists and deficit hawks that will be harsh, partisan, and self-serving.  Who is going to pay for it? This editorial is a nice articulation of this emerging paradigm, dubbed "build and balance", that will put a premium on people as well as products.  

I am learning about this and feel optimistic this is a good direction for us to pursue, both domestically and with allies abroad, as an alternative to the Chinese statist model. The key issue for the consumer is a balance between corporate imperative and a governance imperative on behalf of the little guy. This is no simple feat!

title: This is an important storyline that needs greater public attention.
text: This is an important storyline that needs greater public attention.  Cost of medications is a major concern for Americans, much more than anywhere else in the world. This strategy of Medicare aggressively negotiating with manufacturers, on behalf of patients, is a critical step forward. Initially, it will be for a limited number of drugs but will expand in years to come. Of course the classic pushback from big pharma will be that it’s bad for research & innovation (and corporate profits). What is the balance between public good vs. free market corporate profits? This is an important area that should inform your choice in our country’s politics towards healthcare policy. The other side is running on repealing this as well as the Affordable Care Act! Be smart and critical and data-driven!

title: Dear friends, I strive to keep partisan comments off my page; however, in this election cycle,…
text:
Dear friends, I strive to keep partisan comments off my page; however, in this election cycle, it seems more responsible to offer a clear and comprehensible resource of key facts rather than merely avoiding the issues. Discussions should start with objective facts. Our values and biases, whether inherited or acquired, influence our decisions on which party or platform to support. It's reasonable to discuss and scrutinize the methodology, source, and implications of objective data when justifying a platform. Mark Twain's observations on statistics could well apply to facts in debates.  Of course, if there are "alternate facts", then please do share them so we can be enlightened and update appropriately!  

Steve Ratner's summary on certain pertinent issues provided clarity. I aim to remain active in the coming months, seeking valuable resources to enhance the conversation and ensure accountability from all sides. We recognize that decisions involve trade-offs, yet clarity on objective data is irreplaceable. We are neither ignorant nor blindly conforming; rather, we aspire to learn and refine our thinking.  To be clear, this is NOT a partisan cry but an attempt to be clear about baseline data.

title: This article certainly got my attention!!
text:
This article certainly got my attention!! I am all in favor of getting professional help for mental illness, anxiety, life and relationship 
challenges, etc. The reasons for the seeming prevalence of mental illness are debated, but some clues lie in early childhood experiences, role of trauma, and potentially toxic family dynamics.  The goal of "cognitive behavioral therapy" is to get assistance from a professional to unravel and surface factors involved to develop a healthy balance and perspective on reality to minimize destructive thoughts and behaviors (i.e. shame, guilt, self-sabotage, worthlessness, etc.) and better cope with life.  

This article describes a new dynamic at play in certain therapy circles. The actual suggestion by some therapists to young clients who identify family stress and poor parenting to fully sever relationships (rather than reconcile). I found this to be deeply troubling and shocking.  Will keep an open mind to trends and data in this space and would welcome comments from my discerning friends!

title: As many of you know, I practiced intensive care medicine for many years, where the objective was…
text:
As many of you know, I practiced intensive care medicine for many years, where the objective was to use the best science and technology to support people (keep them alive) at all costs; of course, you also learn the limits of modern medicine and develop an ability to recognize futility and communicate that to families, who are often resistant and in denial. 

Functional literacy about dying and ability to speak about it is important for everyone; any discussion of health and wellness is incomplete without such understanding. Everyone will experience death in their lives (grandparents, parents, etc.); in addition, literacy creates a vocabulary and an opportunity to teach our kids and also express our personal intentions for our own lives. There are many barriers to this.  There is lot more than just a simplistic notion of a health care living will; but much more a dialogue with ourselves and those closest to us to be intentional.

The Aspen Ideas Podcast (and annual conference) is something I recently discovered. This specific episode involves a panel discussing this issue of a "good death." It is not for the faint of heart, as it deals with this issue directly, but I found it provocative!

https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/aspen-ideas-to-go/id702896920?i=1000654966701

title: This is a major advance in medication assisted therapy (MAT) that for some reason is not getting…
text: This is a major advance in medication assisted therapy (MAT) that for some reason is not getting as much exposure as it should!! Of course, narcan as an antidote for opiod overdose is getting the attention it deserves with the opiod pandemic and it is now available over-the-counter as a nasal spray (and for free in community health centers). In addition, naltrexone as a once per day pill Revia (or as a monthly IM shot, Vivitrol) is a safe and effective treatment for those with alcohol or opiate addiction!! Another alternative is acamprostate (camprol).  In some ways, alcohol abuse disorder remains a major problem (perhaps with less stigma than opiod abuse) where MAT should be more widely embraced. There is "resistance" in the traditional AA and 12-step communities. This is a life altering pharmacotherapy for those that can benefit!!

title: Just read Percival Everett's latest book (James: A Novel), after watching his earlier book…
text:
Just read Percival Everett's latest book (James: A Novel), after watching his earlier book "Erasure" adapted into the Oscar nominated film American Fiction. James is a fictional re-telling of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (Twain's seminal work from the 1880s), but from the perspective of Jim (or James in Everett's version), the adult slave friend of Huck the teen! James is re-cast as an educated, scholarly man acutely aware of the hypocrisy living and "passing" in the stereotyped era, rather than just as a kindly but simple and superstitious slave man. 
I found James to be riotously funny, a clever perspective, providing an irreverant look into the absurdity of human bondage (and religion, social mores, etc). Any future high school English curriculum of necessity should assign James as an accompaniment to Huck Finn! Everett pays homage to Twain's vernacular and the story largely tracks with the original till a critical juncture!
This is a quick read and I would highly recommend it for any age reader. I suspect it will be the basis for a future Hollywood film?  The original Huck was banned in many places, so in our hyper-partisan era book-banning may still occur with James?
Best book I have read in many years!

title: This is a timely and compelling read by a leading AI entrepreneur and cofounder of Google's…
text:
This is a timely and compelling read by a leading AI entrepreneur and cofounder of Google's DeepMind. The metaphor of a tidal wave and rapid diffusion of useful technology (steam engines, electricity, cars, cell phones, etc.) globally is apt when applied to the current uptake of AI. 
The Turing hypothesis and Scaling hypothesis are frameworks for how quickly AI will "grow up" based on massive compute power made available.  There is much debate among experts as to timing of artificial general intelligence (AGI), but most range within a decade or two or three!

Author succinctly compares the convergence and explosive growth in computer science/engineering (where bits/bytes and silicon reign) and synthetic biology (DNA, CRISPR, and RNA editing tools); the proposition is for much lower unit cost, ease of use, and hence rapid diffusion. I found this discussion to be strong.

The author spends much time discussing the need for "containment" of this technology to minimize risks (using nuclear weapons as one rare example of humanity attempting to put brakes on technology). In general, his tone is quite balanced and generally optimistic and not alarmist or fantastical. He strongly advocates a greater role for gov't (i.e. establish internal expertise within gov't ranks) as well as civic engagement.

title: Chip War by Chris Miller, 2020)!
text:
Chip War by Chris Miller, 2020)! The is a fast-paced and riveting story spanning 1950s to 2020: of transformative chip industry (silicon valley, term coined in 1971) with emphasis on individuals leading companies, interfaces with global political & military events (cold war stand-off, viet nam war, emergence of Japan, off-shoring for both political and economic reasons,), explosion of uses for chips (guided munitions, computers, servers, mobile phones, cars, and everything), increasing globalization of the value food-chain, hyper-complexity of chip fabrication becoming highly concentrated outside the US, and the rise of China as a competitor and a potential threat! There was extensive coverage of international espionage to obtain latest tech, the failed Soviet "copy it" strategy, the existential threat that Japan and Sony posed to US leadership in the 1980s, the rise of SE Asia as an electronics assembly factory floor, the efforts taken by the US to bar Huawei in China from becoming the next TSMC.

Book traces the invention of Shockley's transistor (Nobel Prize in 1956 to Bell Labs group of 3 scientists), first Integrated Circuit (Nobel to Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments), general microprocessor pioneered by Fairchild and then Intel (heart of the PC revolution), mobile phone revolution, and AI to where we are today. The story focuses on technology pioneered by serious academic entrepreneurs centered in silicon valley, lots of name dropping of who's who, initial role of Pentagon funding, the realization of Moore's Law (rapid miniturization with doubling of transistors for a given size chip), development of photo-lithography for printed circuit boards. The incentive to get rich (i.e. succeed in the market place by increasing volume and lowering costs) and the need for business acumen. 

There is extensive discussion for off-shoring of lower level electronics assembly (initially Japan led my Morita of Sony for transistor radios, calculators, walkmans, digital cameras, S. Korea, Singapore), then production of simple DRAM memory chips, to later highly specialized development of TSMC in Taiwan (led my PM Li and Morris Chang, formerly of TI). Similarly, the complexity of production tools that cost $100M each  to monstrous fab facilities (cost $20B) and the moats that companies develop and the underlying paranoia to maintain market advantage is discussed as well as the rise and fall of Japan and Intel, and how advanced chip manufacturing  largely left the US. 

I learned there are 3 types of chips: 
1. logic chips (used in PCs and servers are x86 architecture, and mobile phones are ARM architecture, or open-source RISC-V), 
2. memory chips (DRAM for short-term or NAND or flash for date/time), and 
3. diffuse/analog chips (sensors to convert audio or image to digital, radiofreq, etc).  

The central processing units or CPUs (made by Intel or AMD) are serial instruction-type for PCs, and graphic processing units or GPUs (made by Nvidia) are parallel processing type for gaming and more recently AI. The chips have evolved into 3D configuration (22 nm, FinFET) to enable greater density and lower power consumption, latest etching tools use 13 nm Extreme UV light (EUV). What is facinating is the hyper-specialization of the industry from chip design in "fab-less" companies (mostly in US), to chip etching tool makers (near monopoly now by the Dutch firm ASML) to chip manufacturing foundries in SE Asia, to parts assembly factory floors also in Asia (each lower in the value chain).

East Asia produces 90% memory chips, 75% logic chips, and 80% of all silicon wafers, with Taiwan (TSMC) making 90% of the most advanced chips! What is clear to me is that redundancy in supply chains is important AND that de-coupling will be nearly impossible.   We are evolving to a "2 party" or bi-polar technology world, with the US side and a China side in both hardware and software to subserve 2 different political world views and governing strategies. There has always been a role for gov't subsidies as well as military application on both sides.  The degree of gov't subsidy is of course far greater in Asia. What is interesting is that economic power, market share, and supremacy are driving factors for both sides, hopefully not in a zero-sum mind-set! How the Taiwan standoff will be resolved remains unknown but seems critical to this industry.

De-risking or de-coupling supply chains is the current mood in the US (for both political parties) on grounds of national military security, but likely for other obvious reasons as well (domestic manufacturing jobs, upper hand in technology to control the future balance of power). What will be the costs to the domestic consumer? where will the workers come from in the US, with an obvious fight over immigration, even legal skilled labor? will new supply routes (i.e. viet nam, India, Mexico) be resilient and cost-effective? All of this is on the table in the near term!

This book is a great read for anyone interested in technology, business of tech companies, global supply chains and off-shoring, national security, and how the world is inter-connected (includes discussion of the recent covid pandemic).  The writer is a policy academic and not a scientist so the book is eminently readable for a non-techie audience!

title: Been reading a lot about disconnectedness and loneliness in our society, as highlighted by our…
text:
Been reading a lot about disconnectedness and loneliness in our society, as highlighted by our Surgeon General Dr Murthy for the past few years.  Issues are complex but structural issues related to our living arrangements plays a role. More community-based living with alternative models of denser living clusters maybe catching on. 

The topic in the WSJ about "forever renters" is less about owning vs. renting in my mind, rather about the model of our living arrangement.  I think there is a broader convo our society is having (with itself) about what constitutes a meaningful way to live our lives! The broader issue is connectedness with other people in our daily lives, esp. with increasing technology, screen time, remote work from home, pandemic of loneliness, etc. This is especially true in the context of job insecurity and the need for multiple job changes in a typical career largely due to structural factors of corporate America. I would submit that the traditional single family homes, a phenomenon of post war years mostly, is quite isolating and does not play into how people are increasingly choosing to live their lives with easily accessible common spaces such as club houses, pools, etc. This is true for both the younger couples with kids as well as the retired set. Denser living arrangements with walkable access to common activities of daily living is what people appear to be gravitating to (not just in highly urban places).

These comments do not address the financial aspects (i.e. long term equity and forced savings of home ownership) as much as the important community aspects. Of course, these alternative cluster living models could be either rentals or owned.

title: What gratifying progress from basic science lab (CRISPR gene editing that proferred a Nobel in…
text: What gratifying progress from basic science lab (CRISPR gene editing that proferred a Nobel in 2020 to Doudna & Carpentier) to 2 newly FDA approved gene therapies (Casgevy and Lyfgenia) for a scourge of a human disease (sickle cell) that torments children and adults; a genetic disease that produces misshapen blood cells can now be cured by a single infusion of a patient’s own stem cells (genetically "spliced and corrected" ex vivo in a lab); the overall therapy preceded by busulfan chemo prep to clear the bone marrow will be arduous and complex (though well-established protocols) and initially ungodly expensive (over $2M, which must be "negotiated" further with state Medicaids hopefully); but first things first, let’s celebrate the accomplishment!! this will be the pathway for many other cures for genetic disorders in years to come!!  I have personally cared for many severely ill patients with acute sickle chest disease on the hospital floors and intensive care units!! will monitor to see how quickly this will be deployed!
